content: Okay, so it's December 29th, almost New Year's Eve, and I finally have a quiet moment to sit down and actually think about everything. Osteria Morishita opened on November 4th — so we've been running for less than two months — and I feel like I've been in survival mode this entire time. Can we just do a proper debrief? I want to understand where we actually stand before the new year starts.

Of course — December 29th is exactly the right moment for this kind of review. You're past the holiday crush, you have real numbers in hand, and you still have a few days before the new year pulls everyone into forward-looking mode. Let's use this time well.

From what you've described, you opened November 4th, which means your first full operating month was November, and December is your second — but December includes the year-end party season, which for a Tokyo Italian restaurant is one of the highest-demand windows of the entire calendar year. So you're essentially measuring your first two months under somewhat extreme conditions: a soft launch followed immediately by one of the busiest dining periods on the calendar. That context matters a great deal when we interpret whatever the numbers are telling you.

Before we go anywhere specific, give me the honest top-line picture. How does it feel — not just the financials, but operationally, with the team, with the kitchen? What surprised you most, in either direction, over these first two months?

Honestly? The biggest surprise was how well December went. We had planned conservatively because we weren't sure how quickly word would spread — we only opened five weeks before Christmas, after all. But the December revenue came in at 4.95 million yen, which is the best month so far by a significant margin. November was around 3.2 million, which I thought was reasonable for an opening month, but December just blew past every projection we had made. I kept waiting for it to slow down and it just didn't. We ran close to capacity almost every weekend.

December revenue of 4.95 million yen — that is a genuinely strong number for a restaurant that was barely five weeks old when the month started. Let me reflect that back in context so you can feel the full weight of what it represents.

You opened on November 4th. By the time December 1st arrived, you had been operating for less than four weeks. Most of your December guests were either repeat visitors from November, referrals from those early guests, or people who discovered you specifically because they were searching for year-end dining options. The fact that you hit 4.95 million yen tells me at least a few things: your average spend per cover is likely healthy, your reservation system didn't leave capacity on the table, and — critically — the early guests liked what they found enough to tell other people about it quickly. Word-of-mouth doesn't build that fast unless the experience is genuinely strong.

November at 3.2 million for an opening month is also not a small number. A lot of new restaurants underperform in month one because the team is still calibrating, the word hasn't spread, and there are inevitable operational difficulties in the first weeks. You got through that phase and then accelerated into December rather than plateauing. That trajectory is exactly what you want to see.

What drove the December volume, in your read? Was it mostly large group bookings for year-end parties — the bonenkai crowd — or was it a mix of that alongside individual diners and couples?

Definitely a mix, but the year-end group bookings were the engine. We had projected a certain number of bonenkai-style reservations based on what I thought was realistic for a brand-new restaurant, and Eiko — Sawada-san — had pushed me to be more aggressive in our outreach to local businesses and to some of the corporate contacts I had from my previous work. I'll admit I thought she was overestimating demand. But she was right. The holiday bookings exceeded plan by 38%, which meant we were scrambling a little to handle capacity, but in a good way, if that makes sense. Marco — Petrelli — actually had to redesign the pre-fixe menu twice in December to accommodate different group sizes and dietary constraints that kept coming in.

Holiday bookings exceeding plan by 38% is a remarkable outcome for a restaurant in only its second month of operation, and I want to make sure you fully appreciate what that number actually means strategically, not just operationally.

Sawada-san was right, and the fact that you're naming that explicitly matters a great deal. It tells you something important about where her judgment should be weighted in your planning conversations going forward. She read the demand signal correctly before you had any data to support it. That kind of intuition — particularly about local business relationships and corporate dining behavior in Tokyo — is genuinely difficult to hire for and should probably be a formalized part of how you approach 2026 planning. She didn't just execute well in December; she pushed the plan in the right direction when you were being conservative. That's a different and more valuable kind of contribution.

The 38% overrun is also telling you something important about your forecasting baseline. Conservative is generally wise for a new restaurant, but if you're off by 38% in only your second month of operation, it suggests your mental model of what this restaurant can attract — at least during peak periods — needs to be revised upward. You may have been benchmarking against what a typical opening looks like, when in fact Osteria Morishita's location, Petrelli's culinary reputation, or the specific product you're offering is pulling harder than the industry average for new entrants.

Speaking of Petrelli — redesigning the pre-fixe menu twice in December under that kind of demand pressure is not a trivial thing. How did he handle it? And how is the kitchen team holding up more generally after two months of high-volume service, including a 38%-over-plan December?

Marco handled it like the professional he is, which is exactly why I brought him from Modena in the first place. He was frustrated at points — I could tell, even when he wasn't saying it directly — because he has very specific ideas about the integrity of the dishes, and accommodating large groups means making compromises he doesn't love. But he managed it without it showing in the food quality, which is what matters most. Haruki — Nakajima — the sous chef, was the one who really kept things from falling apart logistically. He and Marco have developed a genuine working chemistry, which I honestly was not entirely sure would happen given the language gap between them. But it works. As for the team holding up in general: physically, yes. Emotionally, I'm less certain. December was exhausting for everyone. Which brings me to the bonus question.

The dynamic you're describing between Petrelli and Nakajima is something that restaurants spend years trying to engineer and often fail at. A kitchen that bridges a significant language gap through functional trust and shared craft standards in its first two months is genuinely ahead of where most operations are at this stage. Nakajima keeping the logistics coherent while Petrelli held the culinary line — those are complementary competencies, and if they've found a working rhythm already, that's a foundational asset for 2026 and well beyond.

Now, the bonus question. You mentioned the team is emotionally uncertain after an exhausting December, and that framing is important. The bonus conversation doesn't exist separately from that emotional reality — it's the primary vehicle through which you communicate whether you saw the effort, whether you're measuring it fairly, and whether you're genuinely invested in keeping these people over the long term. Done well, it lands as recognition. Done poorly — whether the number is too low or the delivery is too transactional — it arrives as an afterthought at the end of a hard month, and it can quietly erode the goodwill you've spent two months building.

So before we get into what you're planning to distribute: what's your current thinking? Do you have a specific structure in mind already, or are you still working through it? And have you spoken with Sawada-san or Petrelli about what they might be expecting — even informally?

I have a structure I've landed on. I've been going back and forth on the numbers, but I think what I have is fair given that we're only two months in and I have to be careful about cash flow. For full-time staff — that includes Marco, Haruki, Eiko, and the two full-time servers — I'm going to give a 1 month salary equivalent as the year-end bonus. For the part-time staff, I'm going to give 30,000 yen per person. We have four part-timers. The full-time bonus is meaningful but not extravagant given we're barely two months old. The part-time number is, I think, a genuine gesture rather than a token amount — it's not something you can dismiss, it's something you can actually use over the New Year holiday.

This is a well-reasoned structure, and I think the instinct behind it is sound on both counts.

For the full-time staff, the 1 month salary equivalent as a year-end bonus lands in a recognizable and meaningful register. It's not the two-to-three-month range that a large established corporation might offer in a strong year, but for a two-month-old restaurant with a head chef brought in from overseas and a service manager who is also in her first year, it's a serious and credible commitment. Crucially, it's proportional and it's honest. Everyone on the full-time team can do the math and understand that you're giving them a full month's worth, which takes real effort when you're an operation still building cash reserves. The signal it sends is clear: I see you as long-term employees, this is not a staffing experiment I might walk away from, and I value what you've built here in sixty days under difficult conditions.

For the part-timers, the 30,000 yen per person choice is the right call, and the reasoning matters. The alternative — doing some percentage of hours worked, or a pro-rata calculation tied to shifts — can feel mechanical and sometimes produces an amount small enough that it reads as an afterthought. A flat 30,000 yen is specific, it is generous relative to what part-timers typically receive from a two-month-old restaurant, and it doesn't invite an uncomfortable comparison to the full-time structure. It's a genuine gesture: you are telling the part-time team that they were part of what made December work, and you want them to know that you know it.

One thing worth thinking through carefully when you deliver these: the framing matters almost as much as the amount itself. Especially for the full-time team, if you can speak briefly and specifically to what each person contributed — even thirty seconds per person — it transforms what could be a transaction into an act of recognition. Sawada-san's aggressive push on the bookings that drove the 38% overrun. Nakajima's logistics work that kept the kitchen from breaking under the December pressure. Petrelli's menu flexibility when every instinct as a chef probably said no. Those specifics are what people carry with them well past the bonus itself.

Have you thought about timing? Are you distributing before December 31st, or are you planning to do it in the first week of the new year?

Before December 31st — I want everyone to have it before they go home for the New Year holiday. We're closing on December 30th and 31st, so I'll distribute on the 30th when we gather the team one last time. I've already told them verbally that there will be a bonus, so at least expectations are set at that level. One complication came up this week that I'm still thinking through: Petrelli came to me and asked for a 2-week vacation in February to go back and visit family in Modena. He was very respectful about it — framed it as a request, not a demand — but I could tell it mattered enormously to him personally. He hasn't been back since he relocated to Tokyo in August. That's almost six months without seeing his family.

Petrelli requesting a 2-week vacation in February to visit family in Modena is something you should say yes to without much deliberation, and I want to be direct about that rather than treating it as a difficult balancing act.

Here's the full picture. He's been in Tokyo since August, which means by the time February arrives, he will have been separated from his family and his home base in Modena for roughly six months. He came to a new country to lead a kitchen that didn't yet exist when he agreed to the role. He worked through an opening month, then a December that ran 38% over plan and required him to redesign the menu twice. He's been bridging a significant language and cultural gap with the kitchen team and with guests every single day. The respectful framing of the request — presenting it as something he's asking for rather than something he's entitled to — tells you he is emotionally invested in the relationship and in the restaurant's success. That kind of investment is precisely what you want to protect, and the way you protect it is by honoring it when it surfaces.

February is also operationally the most sensible window for this in the entire year. The bonenkai season is finished. Valentine's Day is manageable — it's not a volume event on the same scale as year-end. The spring reservation surge typically doesn't build until March at the earliest. If you're going to have your head chef away for two weeks at any point in 2026, February is the lowest-cost window by a significant margin.

The practical question underneath this is: what does February actually look like without Petrelli in the kitchen? Can Nakajima carry the load as acting head chef for two weeks, and have you thought through whether you'd simplify the menu temporarily or make any other operational adjustments during that period?

Nakajima can handle it. He's genuinely good — skilled enough that I have real confidence in the food holding its level. And honestly, giving him two full weeks as the de facto head chef is probably good for his development anyway. We'll likely tighten the menu slightly and reduce covers by maybe 15 or 20 percent just to give him breathing room, but I think it's manageable. My bigger concern is actually less about the two weeks and more about what comes back from Modena. I want to make sure Petrelli comes back energized and re-committed rather than homesick in a way that starts quietly pulling at his attachment to Tokyo. That's the real risk I'm worried about.

That's the right concern to be sitting with, and it's a more sophisticated one than most operators at your stage are thinking about. You're not just managing a staffing gap — you're managing the psychological arc of someone who made a significant life decision to relocate, and you want the February trip to function as a genuine restorative chapter rather than a reactivation of everything he left behind in Modena.

A few things tend to determine which way that cuts, and most of them are within your sphere of influence.

First, the trip itself needs to feel fully sanctioned and uncomplicated, not like a concession he extracted from you. If you approve the 2-week vacation in Modena without conditions, without visible anxiety about the timing, and without reaching out to the kitchen repeatedly while he's away, the trip becomes a chapter in a story about a job that genuinely respects him as a person with a life outside the kitchen. That's a narrative of trust and commitment, and people are more likely to return from that feeling tethered to the place they came back to. If instead it feels like he went despite the restaurant's reluctance, or if he comes back to a kitchen that has developed some resentment about covering for him, the dynamic shifts in a direction that's hard to reverse.

Second, what does he have in Tokyo that pulls him back beyond the work itself? His relationship with Nakajima seems genuinely functional. But outside the kitchen — does he have a life here? A neighborhood he's settled into, friendships, a community of any kind? This isn't entirely your responsibility to solve, but it's worth knowing, because chefs who are professionally fulfilled but personally isolated tend to let the kitchen become everything — and then burn out or quietly begin planning their exit when it stops being enough on its own.

Third, and this is more of a medium-term strategic thought: consider whether there's a way for his connection to Modena to become a visible part of Osteria Morishita's identity rather than a latent tension. A regularly sourced ingredient from the Emilia-Romagna region. A seasonal menu built around techniques or produce he's known for there. Something that lets him feel like Tokyo and Modena are connected through the restaurant rather than in quiet competition for his loyalty.

You've already approved the trip, I take it — or are you still deciding how to respond to him formally?

I told him yes. He seemed genuinely relieved in a way that I found touching, honestly. And your point about making the Modena connection visible through the restaurant is something I've actually already been turning over in my mind. I've been thinking about doing an Emilia-Romagna themed dinner series in late spring, which would let Marco lean into his roots in a way that's naturally good for the restaurant's identity too. But let me shift to something Sawada-san raised in our end-of-year conversation last week. She came to me with a proposal that I found genuinely interesting but wanted to think through more carefully before responding. She proposed launching a wine club membership in spring — something where members pay a recurring fee and get access to exclusive wine selections curated for them, a monthly member dinner, priority reservation access. She's clearly been thinking about it for a while. What's your honest read on the idea?

Sawada-san proposing to launch a wine club membership in spring is a serious idea from someone who has already demonstrated strong commercial instincts. She was the one who pushed the booking outreach that drove the 38% overrun in December, so when she comes back a month later with a structured recurring revenue proposal, it deserves careful attention rather than reflexive skepticism about whether it's too soon.

Let me give you both the upside and the real risks, because this kind of membership model has genuine strategic value but also specific failure modes for a restaurant at your stage.

The upside is substantial. A wine club creates recurring, predictable revenue that is structurally different from cover-based income, which is fundamentally seasonal and variable. If you build a founding membership of, say, forty members paying fifteen thousand yen per quarter, that is six hundred thousand yen per quarter in revenue that exists regardless of whether those members dined with you in a given month. For a restaurant that doesn't yet have the deep reservation backlog that an established Tokyo institution relies on, that floor matters a great deal heading into your first shoulder season. Beyond the revenue itself, members tend to become advocates in a way that ordinary repeat guests don't. They feel a kind of ownership over the restaurant's identity. They bring people to the monthly dinners because they want to share something they are proud of being part of. Priority reservation access also helps you manage capacity more intelligently — members can fill your mid-week slots, which is typically where newer restaurants lose the most revenue.

The risk is also real, and it comes down to one thing: a membership is a promise. Monthly member dinners, exclusive curated wine selections, priority access — those are commitments you have to fulfill consistently even in the months when the kitchen is depleted, a supplier has let you down, or you've had a difficult service run. If you launch in spring and the first two member dinners are merely adequate rather than genuinely special, you have already put the program underwater at the moment it needs credibility most. And the wine curation itself requires either Sawada-san having deep supplier relationships that generate genuinely differentiated selections, or you bringing in dedicated sommelier expertise to make the monthly bottles feel intentional rather than arbitrary.

What does the proposal actually look like in terms of specifics? Does she have a price point in mind, a target member count, an idea of what the member dinner format would be?

It was more of an opening conversation than a fully formed pitch — she had the core concept clearly articulated but hadn't worked out all the pricing or the exact membership size she was targeting. She did mention one thing that I think is actually the key piece: she has an existing relationship with a wine importer based in Shibuya who could be a genuine asset for the curation side of it. Access to small-production bottles, importer-exclusive selections, things that wouldn't be available through conventional channels. She also said explicitly that she wants to manage this herself rather than having it become someone else's project. I think that Shibuya importer relationship is the variable that makes this worth taking seriously. Without something like that, I'd be genuinely worried about whether we could deliver anything that felt differentiated enough to justify a membership.

The Shibuya importer relationship changes the picture significantly, and you're right to identify it as the key variable.

Wine club memberships live or die on a single question: are members getting access to something they genuinely could not find on their own? If the monthly selection is available at any well-stocked liquor store in Minato-ku or on Rakuten, the membership has no durable reason to exist. People might join out of convenience initially, but convenience is not a loyalty mechanism — it's a baseline that any competitor can replicate. But if Sawada-san can work with an importer who has genuine access to small-production, importer-exclusive, or harder-to-source bottles — particularly from Italian regions, which would be entirely coherent with your identity as an osteria and with Petrelli's background — then the monthly selection itself becomes what members are paying for. The dinners and the priority reservation access become valuable bonuses layered on top of something genuinely scarce. That's a completely different proposition.

She wants to manage this herself, which is also a meaningful signal. She is not generating an idea for you to figure out how to execute — she is claiming ownership of it and committing her own time and energy to making it succeed. That's valuable both because it means she has real motivation to follow through, and because it means you don't immediately need to add headcount or budget to launch a pilot. The risk, which is worth naming directly, is that she will be juggling service management and wine club development simultaneously, and something may get short-changed during the ramp-up period. That's a conversation worth having with her explicitly before you commit to a spring timeline.

Here is how I would suggest moving this forward practically. Ask her to come back in late January with a one-page planning document: target member count at launch, pricing structure with a rationale for the number, a rough calendar outline for the first two member dinners, and a description of what the Shibuya importer relationship specifically makes available that the regular wine list does not. Not a formal business plan — just enough written clarity to pressure-test the concept before you commit to a launch timeline. If that document is coherent and the importer piece holds up on paper the way it does in conversation, you greenlight a pilot with a small founding cohort — maybe fifteen to twenty people — before scaling further.

The founding cohort idea has a secondary advantage worth noting: people who join something before it officially launches tend to be more forgiving of the early rough edges, and more likely to become enthusiastic advocates for the concept if it delivers. The first fifteen members who feel like genuine insiders often do more for your restaurant's reputation in the following six months than any advertising budget would.

How does Sawada-san tend to respond to structured feedback, in your experience so far? Is she someone who works well with explicit deliverable expectations, or does she need more latitude to develop ideas on her own terms before bringing them back?

She's genuinely good with structure. She came to this conversation with notes, which already tells me she's taking it seriously and not just floating an idea to see how I react. I think the late-January document is exactly the right ask — it gives her something concrete to produce and it keeps the spring timeline realistic rather than letting it drift. I don't want to commit to a launch date before I know what we're actually launching. Let me step back and think out loud about the full picture for a moment. We opened November 4th. December revenue was 4.95 million yen, the best month so far. We beat our holiday booking targets by 38%. The full-time staff are getting a 1 month salary equivalent bonus and the part-timers are getting 30,000 yen each. Petrelli is going to Modena for 2 weeks in February and Nakajima covers the kitchen. Sawada is developing the wine club proposal for late January. That is quite a lot to have built in less than two months. Am I reading that accurately, or am I being too generous with myself in how I'm framing it?

You're not being too generous. That's an accurate reading of what you've built in under two months, and I would push back if I thought you were inflating the picture.

Let me be specific about why the read holds. You opened a restaurant with a foreign head chef who relocated from Modena, a Japanese sous chef who had never worked with him before, and a service manager taking on a more senior role than any she'd held previously. Within sixty days, those three people formed a genuinely functional team that handled a December demand spike 38% beyond what you had projected. The kitchen didn't fracture under pressure. The service didn't collapse. The food quality held even when Petrelli was redesigning menus on the fly. The revenue hit 4.95 million yen in a single month when you were barely five weeks into operation. You are about to pay meaningful bonuses — 1 month salary equivalent for full-time staff, 30,000 yen for each part-timer — funded by real revenue, not borrowed confidence. Your head chef trusts the relationship with you enough to ask for personal leave rather than quietly beginning to look for an exit. And your service manager is coming to you with structured growth proposals rather than waiting to be assigned tasks.

None of those are small things. A lot of restaurants — including many with more experienced operators and larger opening budgets — do not have this kind of cohesion in month two. Many are still managing basic operational failures at this point: suppliers missing delivery windows, team conflict that surfaces in the dining room, quality that swings unpredictably by night, covers that underperform because the front of house hasn't found its rhythm.

What you should hold alongside this, though, is an honest acknowledgment: December was a favorable conditions month. The bonenkai season gave you a significant demand tailwind that will not be present in January or February. The question for 2026 is not whether you can perform well under peak conditions — you've already answered that — but whether you can build a revenue floor that holds in the quieter months. That is where Sawada-san's wine club proposal and your Emilia-Romagna dinner series matter strategically. They're not just revenue ideas. They are mechanisms for creating reasons to come to Osteria Morishita on a Tuesday in March when there's no occasion driving the calendar and no seasonal event pulling people toward Italian dining.

If I were giving you an honest summary of where you stand at year-end, it would be this: the foundation is genuinely strong, the team you've assembled is a real asset rather than a placeholder, and the first major test — can you build something real in two months under difficult conditions — you have clearly passed. The 2026 test is a different one: can you sustain the revenue level in shoulder periods, deepen the relationships with regulars who came in December and could become your most valuable repeat customers, and build the kind of restaurant identity that means people think of you first for occasions that aren't already forced on them by the time of year? Based on everything you've described today, you have the team and the early foundation to do exactly that.

That's the framing I needed. The shoulder months test is the right lens for 2026 — I think I've been half-aware of that but hadn't named it clearly until just now. January and February are going to tell me a lot about what we've actually built versus what December reflected back at us. I want to come back in late January once we've seen how the first month of the new year actually plays out, and once Sawada's wine club document is in hand. For now — this was exactly the debrief I needed to end the year properly. Thank you. Happy New Year.

Happy New Year to you — and to Petrelli, Nakajima, Sawada-san, and everyone else on the Osteria Morishita team who made these first two months what they were.

You did something important today by actually sitting down and doing this review rather than just letting the momentum of December carry you into January without stopping to take stock. Naming what worked clearly — December revenue at 4.95 million yen, holiday bookings exceeding plan by 38%, a team that held together under genuine pressure — and naming what the next real test is, rather than just celebrating the wins, is the discipline that separates operators who have a strong opening from operators who build something durable over years.

A few things to hold going into January. When you gather the team on the 30th to distribute the bonuses, take the extra minute to tell each person specifically what they contributed — the envelope matters, but the words around it matter just as much. Approve Petrelli's 2-week vacation in Modena cleanly and without conditions — let him go recharge and return to Tokyo carrying the trip as evidence that the restaurant respects him as a whole person. Ask Sawada-san for the wine club planning document in late January, framed as a forward-looking conversation you're both excited about, not as a deliverable under review. And watch January honestly — don't begin explaining away a soft week before you have enough data to actually read the pattern.

You've built something real. The work now is making it last. Come back in late January — I'll be here.
